Support for the Cuban People Travel in 2026: An Explainer

Cuba is a natural destination for U.S. travelers. Its multifaceted culture, fascinating history, and stunning landscapes reveal a land both foreign and familiar.

However, for U.S. citizens, planning a trip to Cuba involves navigating certain legal restrictions. Understanding the rules and regulations surrounding travel to Cuba is essential to ensure fun, safe trip that complies with U.S. law.

In this guide, we explain everything you need to know about traveling to Cuba under the Support for the Cuban People category. We’ll outline the steps necessary to plan a trip that adheres to the guidelines laid out by the regulations.


What is the Support for the Cuban People category?


The Support for the Cuban People category is one of the 12 categories of legal travel to Cuba authorized by the U.S. government. Under this category, travelers are required to engage in activities that support Cubans and promote independence from Cuban government institutions.

This can include activities such as staying in private accommodations (like hotels and casas particulares), dining at privately-owned restaurants (also known as paladares), and engaging in activities led by Cuban citizens, like guided tours, or lessons in dance, cooking, language, art, and more.

The Support for the Cuban People category aims to encourage interaction between U.S. travelers and the Cuban people, fostering cultural exchange and supporting the growth of independent private enterprise in Cuba. By engaging in activities that directly benefit the Cuban people, you’ll contribute to positive social and economic development on the island while complying with U.S. regulations.

You can plan a trip on your own, or get help from our expert team to make sure your itinerary meets the requirements for legal travel to Cuba and directly supports local private enterprise in the process.


Support our Project


Cayos Travel is a reader supported website. Please consider leaving a tip if you appreciate our content.


What is the “General License” for Travel to Cuba?


In the past, U.S. citizens were required to obtain a specific license from the U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to travel to Cuba legally. However, in recent years, most authorized travel to Cuba is conducted under a “general license.”

A general license allows eligible travelers to engage in certain categories of authorized travel to Cuba without the need to apply for a specific license from OFAC. The Support for the Cuban People category falls under this general license, provided travelers adhere to the specified requirements and restrictions.

Under the general license, travelers must maintain a full-time schedule of activities that support the Cuban people, which may include educational exchanges, humanitarian projects, or support for private businesses. It’s essential to keep detailed records of these activities to demonstrate compliance with U.S. regulations.


The 12 Travel Categories of Authorized Travel


In addition to Support for the Cuban People, there are 11 other categories of authorized travel to Cuba. These categories include family visits, official government business, journalistic activity, and humanitarian projects, among others. While travel to Cuba for tourism purposes remains prohibited, travelers can still visit Cuba under any of these authorized categories.

Each category has its own set of requirements and restrictions, so it’s important to carefully review the guidelines provided by the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) before planning your trip.


Creating a Legal Itinerary


When planning a trip to Cuba under the Support for the Cuban People category, you’ll need to create an itinerary that demonstrates a commitment to engaging with the Cuban people and supporting independent economic activity. This can include activities such as visiting local markets, attending cultural events, and interacting with Cuban artists, entrepreneurs, and community members. Keeping a detailed record of your itinerary and any interactions with Cuban citizens will help ensure compliance with U.S. regulations.

In addition, you’ll need to avoid any businesses designated as a “restricted entity” by the U.S (mainly hotels that are owned by the Cuban government). Luckily there are lots of great of privately owned hotels, B&Bs, and vacation rentals that can be easily booked online.


Travel to Cuba, Support Locals

Our mission is to make Cuba travel more accessible. Our tools support Cuba’s private sector + conform with U.S. travel rules.


Getting a Cuban eVisa/Tourist Card


Before traveling to Cuba, U.S. citizens are required to obtain a Cuban tourist visa (also known as a tourist card). The visa allows travelers to enter Cuba for up to 90 days. Paper cards can be acquired through your airline, but there is now a convenient eVisa process that allows you to purchase it online in advance of your trip through an authorized vendor like Easy Tourist Card.


What to Expect When Leaving and Re-entering the U.S.


The departure process for U.S.-Cuba flights is no different than the process for any foreign flight. There may be differing weight restrictions for luggage, so if you are planning to bring extra suitcases or donated items, it’s important to check the rules ahead of time.

When returning to the U.S. from Cuba, travelers are typically treated the same as anyone returning from a foreign country. In some cases, customs officials will ask about the purpose of your trip. If this is the case, providing a physical copy of your itinerary to show that you’ve properly documented your activities in Cuba will more than suffice.

You may also be asked about goods you are bringing back from Cuba. While most items are allowed, importing Cuban alcohol and tobacco products is prohibited, even for personal use.


The Bottom Line


Traveling to Cuba under the Support for the Cuban People category offers a unique opportunity to engage with the Cuban people and support independent economic activity on the island. By understanding the legal restrictions surrounding travel to Cuba and following the guidelines outlined in this guide, travelers can ensure a smooth and enjoyable trip while remaining in compliance with U.S. law.

As you plan your trip to Cuba, be sure to thoroughly research the requirements and guidelines provided by the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to ensure that your trip complies with all relevant regulations. By taking the time to plan carefully and document your activities, you can enjoy all that Cuba has to offer while contributing positively to the local community.

So pack your bags, brush up on your Spanish, and get ready to experience the vibrant culture and warmth of the Cuban people firsthand. With careful planning and preparation, your trip to Cuba is sure to be an unforgettable adventure.
